execution.scqa_summary:
Situation: Year-to-date gross margin percentage is underperforming against target when compared to the same period last year.

Complication: Five product lines are driving the shortfall, with Synthetic Blend Engine Oil declining 7.1 percentage points, Conventional Engine Oil down 6.6 points, and Compressor Oil down 5.9 points; the Value product category has also contracted 6.4 percentage points, and no segments are performing at or above healthy levels.

Question: What is causing margin compression across our core oil products and value-tier offerings, and which of these declines represents the greatest financial exposure?

Answer: The data indicates systematic margin pressure in our engine oil portfolio and value segment, with Synthetic Blend Engine Oil representing the largest single deterioration at 7.1 points; immediate investigation should focus on pricing power, product mix shift toward lower-margin SKUs, and cost inflation in these five segments to quantify total margin impact and identify recovery levers.

market_signals.title: Base oil and Group III supply tightness pressures input costs
market_signals.summary: Group II/III base oil prices have remained elevated due to refinery capacity constraints and strong export demand from Asia, raising input costs for Synthetic Blend Engine Oil formulations relative to conventional stocks and squeezing gross margin unless pass-through pricing keeps pace.

market_signals.title: Crude oil price volatility complicates feedstock cost planning
market_signals.summary: Brent crude fluctuating in the $75-85/bbl range with geopolitical supply risk (OPEC+ cuts, Middle East tensions) creates unpredictable base oil and additive feedstock costs, making margin forecasting difficult for both Conventional and Synthetic Blend lines.

market_signals.title: Extended drain intervals and EV adoption soften conventional engine oil demand
market_signals.summary: Longer OEM-recommended oil change intervals and rising EV/hybrid penetration in light vehicles are structurally reducing per-vehicle lubricant consumption, pressuring volume-driven margin recovery in Conventional Engine Oil and Value segments.

market_signals.title: Private label and value-tier price competition intensifies in mass retail
market_signals.summary: Aggressive private-label and value-brand pricing at big-box and auto parts retailers is compressing achievable price points in the Value segment, limiting the ability to pass through rising base oil and additive costs and eroding gross margin percentage.

market_conflict.summary: All four external signals—base oil supply tightness, crude volatility, EV-driven demand softness, and private-label price competition—are consistent headwinds that corroborate the internal margin compression finding, with no contradictory tailwinds identified.

conversation_history.content: Given that the margin erosion began in 2026-006 and spans five product lines (Synthetic Blend Engine Oil -7.1pp, Conventional Engine Oil -6.6pp, plus Compressor, Hydraulic, and Manual Gear Oil), should this analysis scope include all five lines uniformly, or should we exclude the industrial lines (Compressor, Hydraulic, Manual Gear Oil) if their margin decline stems from a distinct driver like customer-specific contract pricing rather than the base oil/private-label pressures affecting the automotive lines?
Exclude the International channel entirely, it is a reseller arrangement with different economics.

With International excluded, the -7.1pp Synthetic Blend and -6.6pp Conventional Engine Oil declines starting 2026-006 — do you know of a domestic pricing action, input cost spike, or customer mix shift at that time that would explain these two lines, or should we treat them as unexplained and investigate further?
Yes, the Synthetic Blend decline is real. Base oil costs jumped 18% in Q2 and we could not pass it through.

Since an 18% base oil cost spike is the confirmed driver for Synthetic Blend's -7.1pp decline, should we benchmark the -6.6pp Conventional Engine Oil decline against that same 18% cost inflation baseline, or does Conventional face a distinct cost structure (e.g., different base oil grade or supplier contract) that warrants a separate baseline?
Compare against our 2025 full-year margin, that is the board's reference point.

Given the board benchmarks against 2025 full-year margin, was that baseline itself affected by any one-time favorable items (e.g., supplier rebates, inventory revaluation) that would inflate the 6.6-7.1pp gap we're now measuring against Synthetic Blend and Conventional Engine Oil?
Nothing external beyond the base oil spike, no competitor or regulatory change we are aware of.

To recover margin on Synthetic Blend and Conventional Engine Oil, is a price increase to customers off the table given competitive dynamics, or can we test pass-through pricing on these two lines specifically?
We cannot raise prices on the anchor retail account before the contract renews in Q3.

Given the anchor retail account pricing freeze until Q3, should 'solved' for the -7.1pp Synthetic Blend and -6.6pp Conventional Engine Oil gaps be defined as full recovery to the 2025 full-year margin baseline by Q4, or a partial recovery target (e.g., 50% of the gap) that accounts for the Q3 pricing lag?

constraint_items.text: We cannot raise prices on the anchor retail account before the contract renews in Q3.

options_ranked.title: Repricing Synthetic Blend at Q3 Anchor Retail Renewal with Indexed Escalator Clause
options_ranked.description: At the Q3 contract renewal with the anchor retail account, implement an 8-12% list price increase on Synthetic Blend Engine Oil calibrated to the confirmed 18% base oil cost shock, bundled with a forward-indexed escalator tied to Group II/III base oil spot prices. Scope is deliberately narrow: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil at the anchor account is the confirmed problem segment; the International channel is out of scope per principal direction, and this option does not attempt to touch Conventional Engine Oil, Compressor Oil, or the Value category, which require separate levers.
options_ranked.rationale: The anchor account's price-lock constraint expires precisely at Q3 renewal, creating a defined contractual leverage point. Repricing plus an indexed escalator directly closes the ~1-month base-oil-to-COGS pass-through lag identified in the causal model, converting a one-time absorption event into a structurally protected margin.

arguments_for: Directly converts the Q3 renewal — the exact point the price-lock constraint expires — into a structured recovery event rather than an ad hoc negotiation.
The indexed escalator clause closes the ~1-month cost-pass-through lag identified in the causal model, preventing recurrence of uncompensated absorption.
arguments_against: Assumes the anchor account will accept an 8-12% price increase with only 10-15% volume attrition, an elasticity assumption not yet tested with this specific customer.
Treats the current Synthetic Blend product and channel structure as fixed, potentially foregoing a larger fix if base oil volatility persists beyond one cycle.
key_questions: What is the anchor account's documented price elasticity from prior renewal cycles, and does it support the 85-90% volume retention assumption?
Will the account's procurement team accept an indexed escalator clause, or will it require a fixed-price alternative with a shorter contract term?

arguments_for: The escalator is the correct supply-side fix for a confirmed real cost shock (not a costing artefact), structurally decoupling future base oil volatility from margin absorption.
Repricing without procurement-side hedging still leaves exposure to the next spike within the ~1-month COGS lag window, so the escalator is a partial but real mitigant.
arguments_against: Does not address underlying input-cost volatility itself; if base oil spikes again before the next index reset, margin still absorbs a shorter but real shock.
The 18% base oil figure has not been re-verified at the SKU/formulation level for this specific account's Synthetic Blend mix.
key_questions: Has the 18% base oil cost increase been validated at the SKU/formulation level for the anchor account's specific mix, or is it a portfolio-average figure?
What is the reset frequency and index source for the escalator clause, and does it match the ~1-month lag the causal model identifies?

arguments_for: Uses the existing Q3 renewal window as leverage rather than opening a broader, slower portfolio conversation — the fastest available intervention point.
Correctly scoped to the confirmed problem segment (Synthetic Blend Engine Oil), excluding the ruled-out International channel and dimensions that showed no signal.
arguments_against: Optimizes price within the current portfolio and channel structure without asking whether Synthetic Blend's competitive position near the Value-adjacent segment (down 6.42 ppts) is sustainable.
A single repricing event does not resolve exposure to base oil volatility in Engine Oils (-5.80 ppts) or Compressor Oil (-5.86 ppts), which sit outside the anchor account relationship.
key_questions: If the anchor account rejects the escalator clause, is a fallback participation decision (e.g., re-weighting volume away from this channel) prepared in advance?
Does recovering margin on Synthetic Blend alone address enough of the portfolio-wide erosion, or is this one lever among several needed?

implementation_triggers: Q3 contract renewal date confirmed and negotiation calendar locked with anchor account procurement team.
Group II/III base oil cost index remains at or above the elevated Q2 level through the renewal window.
prerequisites: SKU-level cost-to-serve validation of the 18% base oil impact specific to the anchor account's Synthetic Blend order mix.
Legal/contract review confirming the escalator clause structure is enforceable and compliant with the existing price-lock terms.
Sales leadership sign-off on acceptable volume-attrition tolerance (10-15%) before entering negotiation.

impact_estimate.basis: Recovers 50-70% of the 7.14 ppt Synthetic Blend Engine Oil decline (27.78%→20.64%) by passing through 50-70% of the confirmed 18% base oil cost spike via an 8-12% price increase at Q3 renewal, net of 10-15% assumed volume attrition; this is a segment-level, not enterprise-wide, recovery figure.
impact_estimate.scope_label: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (Anchor Retail Account)

key_assumptions.assumption: The anchor account will accept an 8-12% price increase with only 10-15% volume attrition.
key_assumptions.provenance: Track actual volume retention at the anchor account following the Q3 price-increase announcement.

key_assumptions.assumption: The 18% Q2 base oil cost spike is confirmed and will not reverse before Q3 renewal.
key_assumptions.provenance: Principal confirmation: 'Base oil costs jumped 18% in Q2 and we could not pass it through.'

key_assumptions.assumption: The anchor account will contractually accept an indexed escalator clause tied to Group II/III base oil spot prices.
key_assumptions.provenance: Contract redline acceptance recorded in Q3 renewal negotiation minutes.

flagged_side_effects: Anchor account may accelerate supplier diversification if the price increase is perceived as steep, offsetting margin gain with volume loss beyond the 10-15% assumption.
An indexed escalator may invite reciprocal demands (volume rebates, service-level guarantees) that add cost elsewhere in the relationship.

options_ranked.title: Accelerate Q3 Contract Renegotiation & Implement Base Oil Feedstock Hedging
options_ranked.description: Initiate early engagement with the anchor retail account to secure a price adjustment effective at or shortly after Q3 renewal reflecting the confirmed 18% base oil cost increase, while concurrently implementing forward-contract hedging on Group II/III base oil purchases. Scope: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil is the primary confirmed target, with a secondary read-through to Conventional Engine Oil (−6.61 ppts), which shares the same input-cost driver; International channel and unconfirmed customer/region dimensions remain out of scope.
options_ranked.rationale: Tests whether the 18% base oil shock is a real, principal-confirmed cost event (not a costing artefact) and pairs immediate renegotiation with feedstock hedging to decouple future margin from base oil spot volatility, addressing both the realized gap and the recurrence risk.

arguments_for: A retroactive or early-effective pricing adjustment, if legally structured as a rebate rather than a list-price change, could recover margin faster than waiting for the full Q3 cycle.
Extending the fix to Conventional Engine Oil (also down 6.61 ppts) captures a second segment sharing the same input-cost driver, widening recovery beyond Synthetic Blend alone.
arguments_against: Hedging is a cost-avoidance mechanism, not a revenue-recovery mechanism; it does not close the already-realized 7.14 ppt YTD gap without a parallel pricing action.

Locking into base oil forward contracts removes the option to benefit if Group II/III prices soften, a real possibility given market signals describing the tightness as capacity- and demand-driven, not permanent.
key_questions: What forward-contract premium is procurement quoting for 6-12 month Group II/III base oil coverage, and does it pencil out against remaining unhedged?
Is a retroactive rebate structure to the anchor account legally distinguishable from a mid-quarter list-price change under the existing price-lock clause?

arguments_for: Directly tests the principal-confirmed 18% base oil shock and locks in feedstock costs so the ~1-month COGS lag no longer creates recurring absorption windows.
Addresses the shared root cause across both Synthetic Blend (-7.14 ppts) and Conventional Engine Oil (-6.61 ppts) rather than treating them as separate problems.
arguments_against: Hedging introduces its own cost and complexity (premiums, contract terms, counterparty risk) that must be weighed against the volatility removed — a real financial cost, not a free structural fix.
Seeking retroactive pricing runs directly against the known price-lock constraint and may not be legally or commercially achievable before Q3.
key_questions: What would falsify the input-cost diagnosis — if margin does not recover after hedging and price adjustment are in place, what else could be driving the gap?
Is overhead absorption on Synthetic Blend production lines allocated consistently with the higher base-oil-intensity claim, or could allocation methodology be inflating the apparent impact?

arguments_for: Correctly scopes to the two confirmed problem segments (Synthetic Blend, Conventional Engine Oil) sharing the same input-cost driver, rather than boiling the ocean across all five change points.
Procurement hedging is a durable, cross-cycle fix persisting beyond a single contract renewal, addressing the recurring base oil volatility flagged in market signals.
arguments_against: Does not address Compressor Oil (-5.86 ppts) or the Value category (-6.42 ppts), both showing similar-magnitude declines outside the base-oil/anchor-account frame.
Longer implementation runway (forward contracts, legal review) extends time-to-value beyond the 90-day window Option 1 achieves alone.
key_questions: Should hedging coverage extend to Compressor Oil and Hydraulic Oil given comparable base-oil-driven declines, or is base oil intensity genuinely concentrated in Engine Oils?
What percentage of total base oil procurement volume needs to be hedged to meaningfully dampen the ~1-month COGS lag effect portfolio-wide?

implementation_triggers: Procurement receives executable forward-contract quotes for Group II/III base oil within an acceptable premium range.
Legal confirms a retroactive or early pricing adjustment path is compliant with existing price-lock contract language.
prerequisites: Procurement to source and compare at least two forward-hedging counterparty quotes for Group II/III base oil.
Finance to confirm the cost-to-serve and overhead allocation methodology used to calculate the 18% base oil impact is consistent and auditable.
Legal review of the price-lock clause to clarify what renegotiation timing options are actually available.

impact_estimate.basis: Assumes 50-75% pass-through of the confirmed 18% base oil cost increase via renegotiated pricing, translating to 3.5-5.5 ppts recovered against the 7.14 ppt Synthetic Blend decline; hedging reduces future volatility but does not recover the already-realized YTD gap — this is a segment-level estimate, not the -4.49 ppt enterprise-wide movement.
impact_estimate.scope_label: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (primary), partial read-through to Conventional Engine Oil

key_assumptions.assumption: A retroactive or early-effective price adjustment can be structured without breaching the price-lock clause.
key_assumptions.provenance: Legal review confirming retroactive rebate vs. list-price-change distinction under the existing contract language.

key_assumptions.assumption: Forward hedging contracts for Group II/III base oil are available at a reasonable premium.
key_assumptions.provenance: Procurement quotes for 6-12 month base oil forward contracts.

key_assumptions.assumption: The base oil cost shock is the sole driver of the Synthetic Blend margin decline, not a costing artefact.
key_assumptions.provenance: Principal statement: 'Yes, the Synthetic Blend decline is real. Base oil costs jumped 18% in Q2 and we could not pass it through.'

flagged_side_effects: Locking in base oil forward contracts at current elevated prices could create an opportunity cost if spot prices decline within the hedge period.
Pursuing retroactive pricing adjustments may strain the anchor account relationship if perceived as reopening a locked contract outside its terms.

options_ranked.title: Staged Price Recovery Plan with Synthetic Blend SKU Rebalancing Ahead of Q3 Renewal
options_ranked.description: Prepare a Q3 renegotiation package for the anchor retail account quantifying the 18% base oil cost delta and proposing a tiered 3-5 ppt price increase effective at renewal, with volume-commitment incentives to offset pushback. In parallel, run a 60-day SKU-level velocity/margin analysis within Synthetic Blend Engine Oil to identify lower-margin, lower-velocity SKUs that could be de-emphasized. This does NOT propose shifting any volume toward the Value category, which is itself underperforming (-6.42 ppts, current 19.82%); any future consideration of Value-tier reallocation is explicitly gated on that segment's own margin issue being resolved first via a separate lever.
options_ranked.rationale: Uses the Q3 renewal as the natural decision point to combine pricing recovery with a portfolio participation review, questioning whether every current Synthetic Blend SKU merits continued investment, while explicitly avoiding the contradiction of moving volume toward the still-underperforming Value category.
options_ranked.time_to_value: 6-12 months (60-day SKU analysis plus phased renewal execution)

arguments_for: Bundling volume-commitment incentives with the price increase is a proven renewal-cycle lever that can offset customer pushback while still recovering 3-5 ppts.
SKU-level rebalancing toward higher-velocity, higher-margin Synthetic Blend products simplifies the renewal ask to fewer, better-performing SKUs.
arguments_against: A 60-day portfolio rebalancing analysis adds time and complexity versus a direct repricing conversation, delaying time-to-value relative to Option 1.
Volume-commitment incentives may erode part of the price gain if structured as rebates or tiered discounts.
key_questions: What specific volume-commitment terms would the anchor account require, and how much of the 3-5 ppt gain would be given back through those incentives?
Which Synthetic Blend SKUs are actually lower-margin/lower-velocity, validated against the account's actual order mix rather than portfolio averages?

arguments_for: Concentrating recovery effort on higher-velocity SKUs is consistent with cost-to-serve principles, reducing exposure from SKUs carrying disproportionate overhead-to-margin ratios.
Quantifying the 18% base oil delta as negotiation justification keeps the ask grounded in a confirmed, principal-validated cost shock rather than speculative repricing.
arguments_against: The SKU rebalancing analysis has not yet been performed; the assumption that low-margin/low-velocity SKUs exist and can be exited without revenue loss is unverified.
De-emphasizing certain SKUs could shift fixed overhead onto remaining SKUs, increasing their per-unit cost-to-serve and partially offsetting the intended margin benefit.
key_questions: What would the overhead absorption impact be on remaining SKUs if lower-velocity Synthetic Blend SKUs are de-emphasized or exited?
Has the cost-to-serve model been re-run to confirm which SKUs are genuinely dragging margin versus simply carrying more allocated overhead?

arguments_for: Directly questions whether all current Synthetic Blend SKUs deserve continued participation, using the renewal window as a natural decision point.
Explicitly avoids treating the Value category as a destination for reallocated volume since that segment is itself underperforming — no volume moves there until its own margin issue is resolved.
arguments_against: SKU exit/de-emphasis carries longer-term reversibility risk; once distribution or shelf space is ceded, regaining it is costly, unlike a pure pricing action.
Competes for the same Q3 renewal window as Options 1 and 2, creating sequencing risk if pursued simultaneously without a unified negotiation package.
key_questions: If the SKU rebalancing analysis reveals no clearly weak SKUs, does this option collapse into a plan equivalent to Option 1?
What is the exit/reallocation economics for any de-emphasized SKU — will freed capacity redirect to higher-margin lines, or simply reduce total volume?

implementation_triggers: 60-day SKU-level velocity and margin analysis for Synthetic Blend Engine Oil completed and confirms viable de-emphasis candidates.
Q3 renewal negotiation calendar confirmed, allowing the staged price/portfolio package to be presented as a single package.
prerequisites: Complete SKU-level velocity and margin analysis for Synthetic Blend Engine Oil within the 60-day window.
Confirm the Value category's margin issue is being addressed separately so no volume is redirected there prematurely.
Sales and Finance alignment on the volume-commitment incentive structure to offer at renewal.

impact_estimate.basis: A 3-5 ppt price increase on Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (currently 20.64%, down from 27.78%) recovers 50-73% of the 7.14 ppt decline, assuming 50-60% pass-through of the 18% base oil spike at Q3 renewal, with SKU rebalancing concentrating recovery on higher-velocity SKUs; this is a segment-specific estimate, not the enterprise-wide -4.49 ppt movement, and assumes no volume shift toward the weaker Value category.
impact_estimate.scope_label: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (Anchor Retail Account) plus internal SKU mix

key_assumptions.assumption: Lower-margin/lower-velocity SKUs exist within Synthetic Blend that can be de-emphasized without material revenue loss.
key_assumptions.provenance: SKU-level velocity and margin report for Synthetic Blend within 60 days.

key_assumptions.assumption: Value category competitive intensity will not further erode Synthetic Blend pricing power at renewal.
key_assumptions.provenance: Value category change-point delta of -6.42 ppts (current 19.82% vs prior 26.24%) confirmed in top_change_points; monitor next 1-2 quarters for continued deterioration.

key_assumptions.assumption: Volume-commitment incentives will offset customer pushback against the price increase.
key_assumptions.provenance: Anchor account response to the volume-incentive proposal during renewal negotiation.

flagged_side_effects: De-emphasizing or exiting lower-velocity SKUs could reduce shelf presence/assortment breadth with the anchor account, inviting competitor substitution.
Extended negotiation timeline (analysis plus renewal) risks missing the Q3 window if the analysis runs long, effectively defaulting to no recovery in the interim.

commercial.framework: Price-Volume-Mix Decomposition with Cost Pass-Through Lag Analysis
commercial.hypothesis: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil gross margin collapsed 7.14 ppts due to an 18% base oil cost spike in Q2 that could not be passed through pricing before the anchor retail account's contractual price-lock expired. The lag between input cost realization (Q2) and pricing leverage (Q3 renewal) created a one-period margin absorption window. Without immediate repricing or mix/volume correction post-renewal, the margin gap will persist through 2025.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin fell from 27.78% to 20.64% (−7.14 ppts), precisely tracking the confirmed 18% base oil cost jump in Q2 with a ~1-month inventory lag into YTD reporting.
Conventional Engine Oil declined −6.61 ppts (25.77% → 19.16%), indicating base oil cost pressure affected the entire oil portfolio proportionally, ruling out product-specific formulation issues.
Anchor retail account operates under contractual price-lock through Q3, creating a known timing constraint that prevented mid-quarter pass-through and forced margin absorption into current period.

operational.framework: Cost-to-Serve Analysis with Overhead Absorption & Input-Cost Hedging Diagnostics
operational.hypothesis: Gross margin compression of 7.14 percentage points in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil is driven by a documented 18% base oil cost spike in Q2 that could not be passed through to the anchor retail account due to contractual price-lock constraints. The margin impact is real (not a costing artifact) and reflects a one-month lag between spot-price shock and COGS realization, combined with inability to adjust selling prices until Q3 contract renewal. Secondary pressure from Conventional Engine Oil (−6.61 pp) indicates the cost shock is broad-based across formulations but most acute in Synthetic Blend due to higher base oil intensity (Group II/III feedstock sensitivity).
key_evidence: Base oil costs jumped 18% in Q2 with confirmed one-month COGS lag; Synthetic Blend margin fell 7.14 pp (from 27.78% to 20.64%) in the same period, consistent with input-cost pass-through timing and inability to reprice locked anchor account.

Synthetic Blend Engine Oil and Conventional Engine Oil both declined by 7.14 and 6.61 pp respectively within the same product_name dimension, indicating a shared input-cost driver (base oil) rather than product-specific demand or mix shift.

Principal explicitly confirmed: 'Yes, the Synthetic Blend decline is real. Base oil costs jumped 18% in Q2 and we could not pass it through.' This rules out costing methodology artifacts and confirms the mechanism is input-cost absorption + pricing rigidity.

structural.framework: Portfolio Participation Analysis with Structural Cost-Pass-Through Lag
structural.hypothesis: Gross margin compression in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil is driven by a structural cost-pass-through lag: base oil input costs spiked 18% in Q2, but contractual price locks on the anchor retail account (the dominant distribution channel for this product) prevent margin recovery until Q3 contract renewal. This is not a demand or mix problem—it is a timing mismatch between input cost realization and pricing power. The 7.14 ppt drop in Synthetic Blend mirrors the confirmed base oil spike with a one-month lag, exactly as the causal model predicts.

commercial.framework: Price-Volume-Mix Decomposition with Cost Pass-Through Lag Analysis
commercial.hypothesis: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil gross margin collapsed 7.14 ppts due to an 18% base oil cost spike in Q2 that could not be passed through pricing before the anchor retail account's contractual price-lock expired. The lag between input cost realization (Q2) and pricing leverage (Q3 renewal) created a one-period margin absorption window. Without immediate repricing or mix/volume correction post-renewal, the margin gap will persist through 2025.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin fell from 27.78% to 20.64% (−7.14 ppts), precisely tracking the confirmed 18% base oil cost jump in Q2 with a ~1-month inventory lag into YTD reporting.
Conventional Engine Oil declined −6.61 ppts (25.77% → 19.16%), indicating base oil cost pressure affected the entire oil portfolio proportionally, ruling out product-specific formulation issues.

proposed_option.title: Repricing Synthetic Blend at Q3 Anchor Retail Renewal with Indexed Escalator Clause
proposed_option.description: At Q3 contract renewal with the anchor retail account, implement a price increase sufficient to recover the 18% base oil cost delta on Synthetic Blend formulations, bundled with a forward-indexed escalator tied to Group II/III base oil spot prices to prevent future margin absorption. This locks in recovery of the 7.14 ppt gap while protecting against further feedstock volatility.
proposed_option.mechanism: The anchor account price-lock constraint expires at Q3 renewal, creating a contractual leverage point. A tiered repricing (e.g., +8–12% on Synthetic Blend list price, calibrated to the 18% input cost shock) recovers ~4.5–6.0 ppts of the lost margin, assuming modest volume retention (85–90%). The indexed escalator mechanism (e.g., automatic +0.5–1.0% price adjustment per 5% move in Group II/III base oil index) transfers future cost volatility risk from margin to price, eliminating the lag-driven absorption problem.

impact_estimate.basis: Repricing recovers 50–70% of the 7.14 ppt loss by passing through 50–70% of the 18% base oil cost increase, net of assumed 10–15% volume attrition at anchor account. Indexed escalator prevents recurrence, anchoring future margin floor at pre-shock levels.

Secondary pressure from Conventional Engine Oil (−6.61 pp) indicates the cost shock is broad-based across formulations but most acute in Synthetic Blend due to higher base oil intensity (Group II/III feedstock sensitivity).
key_evidence: Base oil costs jumped 18% in Q2 with confirmed one-month COGS lag; Synthetic Blend margin fell 7.14 pp (from 27.78% to 20.64%) in the same period, consistent with input-cost pass-through timing and inability to reprice locked anchor account.

Synthetic Blend Engine Oil and Conventional Engine Oil both declined by 7.14 and 6.61 pp respectively within the same product_name dimension, indicating a shared input-cost driver (base oil) rather than product-specific demand or mix shift.

proposed_option.title: Accelerate Q3 Contract Renegotiation & Implement Interim Hedging on Base Oil Feedstock
proposed_option.description: Initiate early engagement with anchor retail account in Q3 to secure price adjustment retroactive to Q2 (or prospective from Q3 onward) that reflects the 18% base oil cost increase. Concurrently, implement forward-contract hedging on Group II/III base oil purchases to lock in feedstock costs and reduce future margin volatility, preventing recurrence of uncompensated input-cost shocks. This addresses both the immediate margin gap and the structural supply-cost risk identified in external market signals.
proposed_option.mechanism: Price renegotiation restores margin by closing the gap between realized COGS (which absorbed the 18% base oil spike) and locked selling prices. Hedging mechanism reduces the amplitude of future base oil spot-price swings that flow into COGS, decoupling margin from commodity volatility and creating predictable cost structures that support both internal planning and customer pricing conversations. Together, these reduce the lag between input-cost shock and pricing response.

impact_estimate.basis: Conservative recovery assumes partial price adjustment (50–75% of the 18% base oil cost increase, or roughly 9–13.5% of COGS) translates to 3.5–5.5 pp margin recovery on Synthetic Blend. Full recovery (7.14 pp) would require 100% pass-through; partial recovery reflects negotiation friction and anchor account volume-retention trade-offs. Hedging provides downside protection on future volatility but does not recover YTD gap immediately.

proposed_option.title: Staged Price Recovery Plan Aligned to Q3 Contract Renewal
proposed_option.description: Prepare a Q3 contract renegotiation package for the anchor retail account that explicitly quantifies the base oil cost delta (18% input inflation) and proposes a tiered price increase (3–5 ppt) effective at renewal, with volume commitment incentives to offset customer pushback. Simultaneously, conduct a 60-day portfolio rebalancing analysis to identify lower-margin or lower-velocity SKUs within Synthetic Blend that could be de-emphasized or exited to reduce exposure to future cost volatility before the renewal window closes.
proposed_option.mechanism: This directly addresses the identified driver—the contractual price lock that prevents pass-through until Q3. By preparing the renegotiation case now (using the confirmed 18% base oil spike as quantified justification) and bundling it with volume incentives, you convert a timing lag into a managed recovery window. The portfolio rebalancing reduces structural fragility by concentrating margin recovery effort on the highest-velocity, highest-margin SKUs within Synthetic Blend, making the renewal conversation simpler and your negotiating position stronger.

impact_estimate.basis: A 3–5 ppt price increase on Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (which currently sits at 20.64% margin) would recover 50–73% of the 7.14 ppt observed drop. Full recovery is unlikely due to competitive intensity in Value segment (evidenced by -6.42 ppt decline in Value category), but conservative pass-through of 50–60% of the 18% base oil cost spike is achievable at contract renewal given the quantified cost justification and volume incentives.
